summary: This informational memo describes how an email client should handle voice and fax messages, including those sent using the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM). It gives guidance on what a receiving client should expect and do with such messages.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes email carries a voice message instead of text. This document explains how an email program should treat these talking messages so they play properly.

questions: how should email clients handle voice messages
voice profile for internet mail client behaviour
how should voice messages appear in email
when should a voice message be marked as read
how should clients display message duration
subtitle: How email clients should display and handle voice and fax messages.

tldr.problem: Email clients traditionally handle text. When voice and fax messages arrive via email, clients display them poorly: showing file sizes in kilobytes (not duration in seconds), opening text editors instead of audio players, and marking messages as read before the audio plays.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4024 specifies client behaviors for mixed-media messages. Clients should determine the primary content type (voice, fax, or text) from message headers, and then display appropriate icons, open appropriate viewers, show appropriate sizes, and mark as read only when the primary content is viewed.
tldr.outcome: Email clients that follow this guidance provide a consistent, intuitive experience for voice and fax messages, similar to the experience for text messages.

today: RFC 4024 is an Informational RFC published in July 2005. It remains a reference for client implementations that handle voice and fax messages, though many modern email clients have not fully adopted these behaviors for web and mobile interfaces.

sections.title: Voice and Fax in the Mailbox
sections.content:
RFC 4024 defines expected behavior for messaging clients when handling voice and fax messages, particularly those formatted as VPIM (Voice Profile for Internet Mail) messages. As unified messaging systems integrate voicemail, email, and fax, clients must learn to handle multiple media types in the same message.

A key concept is Message-Context, a header field that declares the primary content type of a message—voice, fax, or text. For messages with multiple parts (for example, a voice message with an attached text transcript), the Message-Context identifies which part is the main content.

The RFC acknowledges that messaging clients have evolved beyond graphical interfaces on computers. Modern clients include text-based interfaces on wireless devices, web clients, and teleset user interfaces (TUI) where messages are listened to over a telephone. Despite this diversity, user expectations remain consistent: a voice message should behave like a voice message, whether accessed from a desktop, phone, or web interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When a voice message arrives, the email program needs to know it's a voice message. Then it can treat it right: show a phone icon, play it with sound, tell you how long it is, and remember when you've listened to it.

sections.title: Displaying Messages Correctly
sections.content:
A messaging client should display a visual or audio cue to indicate the message type. For graphical clients, obvious choices are a telephone icon for voice, a fax-machine icon for fax, and an envelope for text. For teleset interfaces, an audio cue or earcon like a spoken prompt "voice message" is appropriate.

The icon can be enhanced to show read status. A telephone with the receiver off-hook might indicate a played voice message. A fax machine with paper at the bottom (rather than the top) might show a viewed fax. An open envelope shows a read text message.

In a message list showing multiple messages, clients should display the sender's phone number for voice and fax messages, rather than forcing it into an email address format. This is critical for users who want to return a call. A separate column or header field makes this number visible without converting it to an email address.
sections.plainLanguage: Show a phone for voice, a fax machine for faxes, and a letter for email. Show the caller's phone number so you can call them back. Change the icon when you've listened to it.

sections.title: Showing Message Size Appropriately
sections.content:
Message size is traditionally shown in kilobytes. For voice messages, kilobytes are not meaningful; a user cares about duration in seconds. For fax messages, the relevant information is the number of pages. Text messages remain measured in kilobytes.

The RFC proposes three methods to relay this information. The first and preferred method uses the Content-Duration MIME header (defined in RFC 2424) for voice messages. For fax messages, a new MIME header called Content-Page-Length could specify the number of pages.

Alternatively, length information can be embedded as a parameter in the Content-Type header (for example, Content-Type: audio/*; length=50) or in the message's Subject line (for example, Subject: Voice Message (0:04)). The first method is preferred because it separates metadata from human-visible fields and works naturally with IMAP.

When a message contains multiple audio or fax parts, the client may display the main part's duration or an aggregate of all parts, depending on implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Show voice messages in seconds, faxes in page count. Don't say "500 kilobytes" for a voice message—that doesn't help you decide if you have time to listen.

sections.title: Opening the Right Viewer
sections.content:
When a user opens a message, the client should open the appropriate viewer for the primary content type: an audio player for voice, an image viewer for fax, a text editor for text messages. The Message-Context header tells the client what the primary type is.

Where multiple viewers are available for one media type, the user should be prompted to choose on the first encounter. That choice becomes the default for that media type going forward, and the user can change the default at any time.

The viewer may or may not be part of the client itself. A user might select to play a voice message from a graphical email client but have it play over a telephone speaker (because the user has no desktop speakers). Similarly, a user listening to their inbox over a teleset interface might choose to print a fax message to a nearby fax machine instead of listening to it read aloud.

When a message contains multiple body parts, the viewer used depends on which part the user selects.
sections.plainLanguage: Click a voice message and it plays. Click a fax and it opens an image viewer. Click text and it opens an editor. The first time, pick your favorite viewer; next time it opens automatically.

sections.title: Marking Messages as Read
sections.content:
Users need to know which messages they have read and which are unread. Traditionally, email clients mark a message as read as soon as the first body part (typically text) is viewed.

For voice and fax messages, this is incorrect. A voice message should not be marked as read until the audio part has been played. A fax should not be marked as read until the image has been viewed.

For IMAP4 clients, this means delaying the setting of the \SEEN flag until after the primary content type (as indicated by the Message-Context header, or by content-disposition or content-criticality headers) has been opened. If the message context indicates a voice message, the flag is set only after the primary voice part is opened. If the context indicates a fax, the flag is set only after the fax image is opened.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't say you've read a voice message until you've actually listened to it. Don't say you've read a fax until you've looked at the picture. Mark as read only when the main content is actually viewed.
